reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive disorder chiefly caused by variants in SH3PXD2B, affecting bone, eye and heart development
Craniofacial features include brachycephaly, a prominent forehead, wide fontanelles, hypertelorism and full cheeks
The characteristic eye finding is megalocornea, often with congenital glaucoma, threatening vision if unrecognised
Skeletal features include bowing of the long bones, prominent coccyx, flexion deformities and generalised joint or bone anomalies
Congenital heart defects are frequent and contribute to morbidity
It overlaps with Melnick-Needles syndrome and other frontometaphyseal/otopalatodigital-spectrum disorders, which enter the differential
Management is supportive with early ophthalmic assessment for glaucoma, cardiac evaluation and orthopaedic care
reference.pathophysiology: Frank-ter Haar syndrome is most often caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in SH3PXD2B, an adaptor protein that organises podosomes, the actin-rich structures cells use to remodel the extracellular matrix. Impaired podosome function disturbs matrix turnover in developing bone, eye and cardiovascular tissue. This produces the skeletal anomalies with bowing and flexion deformities, the megalocornea and glaucoma from abnormal anterior-segment development, and the congenital cardiac defects that together define the phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Other syndromic skeletal dysplasias with eye involvement
additionalInvestigations: SH3PXD2B sequencing, ideally within a relevant gene panel
Ophthalmic examination for megalocornea and intraocular pressure measurement for glaucoma
Skeletal survey for bowing, flexion deformities and other bone anomalies
redFlags: Congenital glaucoma with raised intraocular pressure risking irreversible visual loss
Respiratory or feeding difficulty in infancy
reference.prognosis: Outlook varies with the severity of cardiac and skeletal involvement; some infants have serious complications early in life, while others survive into childhood and beyond with careful multidisciplinary management, and vision depends on prompt glaucoma treatment.
pitfalls: Missing congenital glaucoma behind an apparently large, clear cornea
Confusing it with Melnick-Needles or other otopalatodigital-spectrum disorders
Overlooking a significant congenital heart defect
Failing to arrange molecular confirmation to guide recurrence-risk counselling
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Urgent ophthalmological management of congenital glaucoma with intraocular-pressure-lowering therapy and glaucoma surgery to preserve vision, with lifelong monitoring of the megalocornea
Cardiological assessment and treatment of congenital heart defects, including surgical correction where indicated
Orthopaedic and physiotherapy management of long-bone bowing, flexion deformities and joint contractures, with corrective surgery as needed
Regular surveillance of growth, development and progression of skeletal deformity
Multidisciplinary coordination across clinical genetics, ophthalmology, cardiology and orthopaedics
Genetic counselling for the autosomal recessive SH3PXD2B-related disorder, with carrier testing and recurrence-risk discussion
